hero.headline: Martin County faces $2.1 billion transportation funding gap over next 20 years
hero.body:
Martin County is facing a $2.1 billion transportation funding shortfall over the next 20 years, a gap that could shape how residents get around for decades. The Martin County Metropolitan Planning Organization estimates the county will need approximately $2.8 billion for transportation improvements through 2050, but only $701 million is currently available. The county can fund just about one quarter of its identified needs. The cost analysis was emailed to county and Stuart officials last August and outlines transportation needs across roads, transit, aviation, freight, and other infrastructure categories.

Nine roads identified by the county as requiring widening remain unfunded as traffic grows. The total cost to widen those roads is approximately $213 million, money that is not currently available, leaving all nine projects out of the county's draft Cost Feasible Plan. The unfunded roads include SW Martin Downs Boulevard, SR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW 96th Street, SW Bridge Road, CR-714/SW Martin Highway, SW Allapattah Road/CR-609, SE Green River Parkway, SW Indiantown Avenue, and SE Bridge Road/CR-708. May and Maddy Brumlow, who travel Martin Downs Boulevard nearly every day, said the congestion is already noticeable. "There's always traffic, it's always backed up," Maddy Brumlow said.

Of the $701 million currently available, all but $10 million comes from state and federal funding sources. Beth Beltran, administrator for Martin County's Metropolitan Planning Organization, said funding shortfalls of this scale are not unusual. "I don't think I know of one MPO in the whole country where the needs are equal to the revenue," Beltran said. She explained that local governments routinely identify transportation needs and then compete for limited state and federal dollars to fund them. State Road 710 is among the county's highest priorities and has been the subject of repeated safety concerns. "Fatal crashes as well as serious injury crashes were just enormous out there," Beltran said. "So that's about $300 million."

The draft Cost Feasible Plan totals approximately $746 million in year-of-expenditure dollars and covers multiple transportation categories. It includes highway and roadway projects totaling $213.97 million, Turnpike projects at $274.81 million, transit at $160.4 million, complete streets and non-motorized improvements at $34.7 million, and $44.02 million for capital improvements at Witham Field Airport. Cove Road, a route long plagued by heavy traffic, is among the projects that made it into the cost-feasible plan and would be widened from two lanes to four with a shared-use path added. Residents can submit input to the Martin County MPO by contacting Principal Planner Ricardo Vazquez.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce Planning Board reviews Causeway Cove proposal with five high-rise buildings up to 17 stories
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce neighbors packed a planning board meeting Monday to review a development proposal for Causeway Cove that includes a 17-story building standing 192 feet tall, more than four times the city's height limit.
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Planning Board on Monday reviewed the Causeway Cove development project located off Seaway Drive, which includes five high-rise buildings with one reaching 17 stories and standing 192 feet tall, more than four times the city's height limit. Plans also call for two hotels and more than 70,000 square feet of retail space. The project qualifies under the Live Local Act, a state law passed in 2023 that allows developers to bypass height and density restrictions as long as they set aside 40 percent of units for affordable housing for at least 30 years. The development includes more than 900 apartments and condos, with 365 designated as affordable housing.

Neighbors packed the chamber during Monday's planning board meeting to review the plans. Buster Brewster, a boater at Causeway Cove Marina, said he worries the project will change the character of the area. "We're going to put this big old conglomerate up here, and I'm just afraid it's going to take away from the beauty of this place," Brewster said. Dennis Fein attended the meeting and raised concerns about traffic. "Nobody's thought this out," Fein said. "You're going to have massive traffic jams. Nobody's going to be able to get on the island, off the island."

City Planning Director Kev Freeman said developers must add traffic mitigation efforts and any required intersection or access improvements. City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city has no authority over whether the project is approved. "The city does not have a play here. We do not have a position in this. This is regulated by the state of Florida in the entirety. The city has been eliminated from the process," Broderick said.

City commissioners are scheduled to hear a review of the project as the next step in the process. The Live Local Act provisions allow the development to exceed local zoning restrictions because of the affordable housing component, which requires that 365 of the more than 900 residential units remain affordable for at least 30 years.

cards.headline: Rising insurance costs become key election issue for 65% of Florida voters in new study
cards.teaser: A new study from online insurance marketplace Insurify found 65% of Florida respondents said rising insurance costs would make them more likely to vote in the 2026 midterms.
cards.body:
The cost of homeowners insurance is becoming a key political issue as the 2026 midterm elections approach, according to a new study from online insurance marketplace Insurify. The study found 58% of Americans say rising home insurance costs are making them more likely to vote in the 2026 elections. In Florida, that number climbs to 65%. Insurify economist Julia Taliesin said the company wanted to look at whether there was any connection in some of these states between the political environment and insurance regulation.

Insurify puts the Florida statewide average premium at $8,292, with a modest 2% increase expected this year. The study found 84% of Florida respondents plan to vote in the 2026 midterms, with 72% of Florida respondents being homeowners. Additionally, 49% of Florida homeowners reported their home insurance premiums increased in the last 12 months, 57% of Florida respondents feel negative about the state of the economy, and 71% of Florida respondents believe elections affect home insurance costs in their state. Republican state leaders this year have been leading the charge for property tax reform as a new affordability target. Taliesin said insurance complexity may be driving that political shift in focus, noting it demonstrates what is easiest to shift where they can focus and get maybe the biggest result, and insurance is complicated.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie couple fights city rezoning of lot behind home from residential to commercial
cards.teaser: Joseph and Margaret Mucciolo are searching for answers after the Port St.
cards.body:
Joseph and Margaret Mucciolo are searching for answers after the Port St. Lucie City Council voted unanimously Monday to rezone the lot behind their home from residential to commercial, despite their months-long opposition. Margaret Mucciolo said the setting is what drew them to the property. She told the real estate agent to get ready to make an offer because it just felt like home. The views of nature and sense of quiet relaxation pushed them to purchase. Joseph Mucciolo said in six months or a year, it's going to be gone. The council approved changing the lot where trees currently stand to be rezoned from residential to commercial.

One council member said adding commercial closer to neighborhoods reduces the length of trips, which reduces overall traffic because shorter trips reduce the burden on the overall network. The two spoke at Monday's meeting voicing their concerns, but they feel the council left them unheard. Joseph Mucciolo asked where they can go from here and whether they can make an objection and have this looked at again. The council held its second reading Monday as a quasi-judicial hearing, meaning council members act as a panel of judges applying existing zoning rules to a specific property and making decisions based strictly on sworn testimony and factual evidence, not public opinion. Margaret Mucciolo said the process needs to change until it's logical, transparent, caring, and provides hope for people. The couple will be exploring any kind of appeal process.

cards.headline: Florida Democrats point to 30 local special-election wins as proof supermajority is breakable
cards.body:
Florida Democrats point to more than 30 local and special-election wins as evidence they can break Republican supermajorities in the state Legislature, outlining a comeback strategy focused on affordability during a Monday briefing. The party has flipped seats across local offices and recent legislative special elections since the 2024 election, including contests in districts previously carried by President Donald Trump. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said the Republican supermajority in the Legislature is breakable and promised to break it this cycle.

Democrats currently face a steep climb. Republicans hold at or above the two-thirds threshold in both chambers, with a supermajority requiring 80 of 120 House seats and 27 of 40 Senate seats. Republicans also maintain a voter registration advantage of more than 1.5 million, with about 5.54 million active registered Republicans compared to 4.03 million Democrats as of May 31, according to the state Division of Elections. Another 3.32 million voters were registered without party affiliation. Governor Ron DeSantis defeated Democrat Charlie Crist by roughly 19 percentage points in 2022, and Trump carried Florida over Kamala Harris by about 13 points in 2024, the largest Republican presidential margin in the state since 1988.

Democrats are building their message around affordability, blaming nearly three decades of Republican control for rising housing, property insurance, healthcare and everyday living costs. The party is challenging a Republican-backed property tax amendment headed to voters, arguing that cutting local government revenue could threaten services or shift costs elsewhere. Fried said if Republicans wanted to reduce the cost of living for everyday Floridians, they could have done that through the legislative process. Instead, what they're doing is making our local governments the big boogeyman, Fried said. Senate Democratic Leader-designate Tracie Davis said the party has put in place the programs needed to capitalize and break these supermajorities once and for all.

The party attributes its momentum to the Pendulum Project, a year-round organizing operation designed to maintain voter contact between major elections. Democrats report more than 3,000 volunteers, increased candidate recruitment and an advantage in requests for vote-by-mail ballots. Fried said the latest special-election results provide a proof of concept that the party's organizing and affordability message can work. The Florida Democratic Party will hold its Leadership Blue annual gathering July 17 through 19 at Disney's Coronado Springs Resort in Lake Buena Vista, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg delivering the keynote address at the July 18 gala.

cards.body:
Margaret and Joseph Mucciolo purchased their Port St. Lucie home for the backyard views of nature and quiet relaxation. Joseph Mucciolo said in six months or a year, it's going to be gone.

The Mucciolos say they will be exploring any kind of appeal process to change this outcome or to change the next one.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks community support as husband battles head and neck cancer
cards.teaser: Dave and Faren Motz of Hobe Sound are asking for community support as they navigate a cancer diagnosis that has cost them nearly $20,000 out of pocket after nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments.
cards.body:
Dave Motz, a former firefighter, was diagnosed with head and neck cancer just months after he and his wife Faren purchased property and settled in Hobe Sound. The couple had previously met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised their three children. "I was so scared cause I didn't know what to expect," Faren said. As they searched for the right healthcare in Florida, AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource. "It was more about the fact that we had a catastrophic situation that that's what they're there for. So many kind people that gave to their charity, saved my husband's life," Faren said.

Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments. The repeated visits to Orlando, biopsies, scans, and exams added up, costing the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket. Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid. "Some days were good and other days were not," Faren said. Doctors told Dave he has an 85% chance of recovery. Dave, who had long been the family's provider, now relies on Faren's support. "She got me through the surgery, she toughed it out drove me back and forth from Orlando. Just amazing trooper, just love her so much," Dave said. Faren works at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

hero.headline: Czech player Linda Noskova wins Wimbledon women's title after five blown match points
hero.teaser: Linda Noskova overcame Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 in an all-Czech Wimbledon final on Saturday. The 21-year-old wasted five match points in the second set before recovering for her first Grand Slam trophy.
hero.body:
Linda Noskova recovered from a second-set meltdown in which she wasted five match points to overcome Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 in an all-Czech final on Saturday for her first Grand Slam trophy. The 21-year-old became the third Czech woman in four years to win the grass-court major, after Marketa Vondrousova in 2023 and Barbora Krejcikova in 2024.

Petra Kvitova, who won Wimbledon in 2011 and 2014, was in attendance, as was Martina Navratilova, who won a record nine singles titles at the All England Club. Navratilova looked on from the Royal Box, where she was seated next to Kate, the Princess of Wales, who was due to present the Venus Rosewater Dish trophy to Noskova. Muchova and Noskova played doubles together at the 2024 Paris Olympics and finished fourth. In the men's final on Sunday, top-ranked Jannik Sinner will attempt to defend his title against French Open champion Alexander Zverev.

cards.headline: England and Argentina reach World Cup semifinals, face off Tuesday
cards.teaser: England and Argentina advanced to the World Cup semifinals after victories over Norway and Switzerland. The match will be held Tuesday as part of the final four.
cards.body:
England beat Norway with two goals from Jude Bellingham to advance to the semifinals. The 23-year-old scored twice to inspire his team past Erling Haaland's Norway. England has relied on Harry Kane and Bellingham, who have each scored six goals in the competition. The team was last in a World Cup semifinal in 2018 but lost on that occasion to Croatia.

Argentina beat Switzerland in extra time after Julián Alvarez scored to help the defending champion advance to the semifinals. Argentina has relied on Lionel Messi to get out of trouble throughout the tournament, though Alvarez was the star in the quarterfinal. Argentina has scored the most goals out of anyone in the competition with 17. Many members of the current squad won the title in 2022.

The other semifinal features France against Spain. France has been considered the tournament favorite and has waltzed through the rounds, relying on Kylian Mbappé and Ousmane Dembélé. Spain has conceded just one goal the entire tournament. Spain beat France in the semifinals of Euro 2024 and also beat Les Bleus in the Nations League last year.

cards.headline: Jannik Sinner beats Alexander Zverev to win second straight Wimbledon title
cards.body:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner beat Alexander Zverev 6-7 (7), 7-6 (2), 6-3, 6-4 Sunday for his second consecutive title at the All England Club. Sinner's fifth Grand Slam title came in his first tournament since a second-round meltdown at the French Open, when he wilted in a Paris heat wave. When Sinner ripped a forehand winner up the line on his first match point, the Italian dropped to the grass on his back in celebration. A year ago, Sinner beat Carlos Alcaraz in the final at the All England Club after wasting three match points against his rival in the Roland Garros final. It was Sinner's 10th straight victory over Zverev, who was coming off his first Grand Slam title at the French Open.

The match turned at 3-3 in the third set, 2 hours and 42 minutes in, when Zverev earned his first break point of the match. Sinner produced a drop shot and Zverev slipped and appeared to hyper-extend his right knee as he attempted to change directions behind the baseline. Zverev grasped his knee in apparent discomfort and Sinner went around the net and helped his opponent up off the grass. Zverev quickly resumed playing but appeared slightly hampered and slung his racket across the baseline in frustration when he missed a forehand and handed Sinner the first break of the match and a 5-3 lead in the third. Zverev had lost 14 straight sets to Sinner before claiming the opening set of the final with a forehand winner up the line to conclude a tight tiebreaker, letting out a loud roar toward his box as he bent over in celebration.

cards.teaser: Florida regulators told Duke Energy its cost plan for AI data centers is on real shaky ground.
cards.body:
Florida regulators have raised concerns about Duke Energy's proposal to pass costs related to AI data centers on to customers. The regulators told Duke Energy its plan is on real shaky ground, according to reports.

The regulatory pushback comes as energy companies across the country grapple with how to handle the massive power demands of artificial intelligence data centers. Florida regulators are scrutinizing whether utility customers should bear the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve these facilities.

She explained that local governments routinely identify transportation needs and then compete for limited state and federal dollars to fund them. State Road 710 is among the county's highest priorities and has been the subject of repeated safety concerns. "Fatal crashes as well as serious injury crashes were just enormous out there," Beltran said. "So that's about $300 million."

The draft Cost Feasible Plan totals approximately $746 million in year-of-expenditure dollars and covers multiple transportation categories. It includes highway and roadway projects totaling $213.97 million, Turnpike projects at $274.81 million, transit at $160.4 million, complete streets and non-motorized improvements at $34.7 million, and $44.02 million for capital improvements at Witham Field Airport. Cove Road, a route long plagued by heavy traffic, is among the projects that made it into the cost-feasible plan and would be widened from two lanes to four with a shared-use path added. Residents can submit input to the Martin County MPO by contacting Principal Planner Ricardo Vazquez.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks support as Dave Motz battles head and neck cancer
cards.teaser: Dave and Faren Motz moved to Hobe Sound and purchased a property, but just months after settling in, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer.
cards.body:
Dave and Faren Motz met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised their three children. Faren homeschooled their kids and the couple started a business with a farm where they served children. Years later, the couple moved to Hobe Sound and purchased a property, but just months after settling in, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer. The repeated visits to Orlando for treatment, biopsies, scans, and exams added up, costing the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket. Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid.

AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource for the couple. Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments. Dave, a former firefighter, had long been the family's provider, but now Faren has stepped up to support them both, driving him back and forth from Orlando for treatment. Doctors told Dave he has an 85 percent chance of recovery. Faren works at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort, where those who want to show their support can stop by and visit. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

hero.headline: Fire engulfs Ford F-250 pickup on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded to a fully involved vehicle fire Monday morning on Florida's Turnpike Northbound near Mile Marker 175.
hero.body: St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded to a vehicle fire Monday morning on Florida's Turnpike Northbound near Mile Marker 175. Firefighters arrived to find a fully involved Ford F-250 pickup truck on the shoulder of the interstate. Crews initiated an aggressive fire attack, bringing the fire under control while working alongside the Florida Highway Patrol to maintain a safe scene for motorists. Traffic was temporarily impacted as firefighters extinguished the fire and secured the scene. No additional vehicles were involved. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie couple fights city council rezoning of lot behind their home from residential to commercial
cards.teaser: Margaret and Joseph Mucciolo say they feel unheard after the Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously voted to rezone the lot behind their home from residential to commercial.
cards.body:
Margaret and Joseph Mucciolo purchased their Port St. Lucie home for the backyard views of nature and quiet relaxation. Margaret Mucciolo said she saw the beautiful setting and told the real estate agent to get ready to make an offer because it just felt like home. But now the couple says their little piece of paradise is under threat after the city council voted to rezone the lot behind their yard, where trees currently stand, from residential to commercial. Joseph Mucciolo said in six months or a year, it's going to be gone.

The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the rezoning change in a unanimous vote. One council member said adding commercial closer to neighborhoods reduces the length of trips, which reduces overall traffic because trips are shorter and it reduces the burden on the overall network. The couple fought the change for months and spoke at Monday's meeting, but they feel their voices have gone unheard. The council held its second reading Monday as a quasi-judicial hearing, meaning council members act as a panel of judges, applying existing zoning rules to a specific property and making decisions based strictly on sworn testimony and factual evidence, not public opinion. The Mucciolos say they will be exploring any kind of appeal process to change this outcome or to change the next one.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Opens Registration for Free City University Program
cards.teaser:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes
cards.body:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes begin Wednesday, Aug. 12, and will be held from **5:30 to 8:30 p.m. in the Council Chambers at Port St. Lucie City Hall**, located at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

Participants will learn about City departments, municipal services and the decision-making processes that shape the community. The program also gives residents opportunities to meet City staff, ask questions and gain a closer look at the work involved in operating one of Florida's largest cities.

Residents who complete the course will receive a certificate of completion and may also choose to become a City Ambassador, helping share information about City programs and services throughout the community.

City University is intended to encourage civic engagement while strengthening connections between residents and local government. Since the program began in 2016, more than 600 residents have participated.

**Enrollment is limited to 160 participants.**

Residents who are unable to attend the in-person classes can also access City U on Demand, which offers a more flexible way to learn about Port St. Lucie government and municipal operations.

hero.headline: Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse offers 165 years of history with 105-step climb to panoramic views
hero.teaser: The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, built in 1860, offers visitors a 105-step climb to panoramic views of the Atlantic Ocean, Jupiter Inlet, and Loxahatchee and Indian rivers.
hero.body:
The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse stands as a red brick tower at the base of the Jupiter Inlet on Florida's Atlantic coast, constructed in 1860 and operating continuously for 165 years as both an active navigational aid and a public attraction. The historic structure has guided mariners since before the Civil War while welcoming visitors who climb to its observation gallery for sweeping views of the surrounding waterways and coastline. The tower's design requires visitors to follow the same path lighthouse keepers took throughout history to maintain operations.

Reaching the observation gallery at the top of the lighthouse requires ascending 105 steps up a narrow spiral staircase that winds through the interior of the brick tower. This route follows the same path that lighthouse keepers climbed night after night to maintain the powerful Fresnel lens that projected light across the water to passing ships. The spiral staircase leads upward through the tower to the gallery at the top, allowing modern visitors to retrace the steps of the early keepers who ensured the beacon remained operational throughout the decades.

The observation gallery provides panoramic views stretching across multiple waterways and the ocean. The Atlantic Ocean extends to the east, while below the tower, the turquoise waters of the Jupiter Inlet converge with the Loxahatchee and Indian rivers. Visitors at this elevated vantage point can watch boats glide through the channel as sea breezes sweep across the observation area. The commanding perspective reveals why this location proved ideal for a lighthouse, offering clear sightlines across the coastal landscape and waterways that allowed keepers to monitor maritime traffic and project the beacon across miles of ocean.

The museum grounds preserve more than just the tower itself. Restored historic buildings chronicle the lighthouse's journey from its construction before the Civil War through its years as an active Coast Guard station. These structures provide information about the lighthouse's role in regional maritime history and offer details about the daily lives of the keepers who operated the station. The site maintains the supporting buildings that allowed the lighthouse station to function across more than a century and a half of continuous service, preserving the complete story of this working navigational aid that has marked the Florida coastline for generations of mariners.
